conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___, one of your hospitalists. You've just come back from your bronchoscopy, and I wanted to check in on how you're feeling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’m okay, still a bit groggy. My chest feels sore, especially near the trach site. But I can breathe fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. The procedure involved dilating some narrowed areas in your airway, so some discomfort is expected. The team noted mild stenosis just below your trach, and the left main stem was quite tight — they opened it up to 9mm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the bronchus intermedius? Was that narrowed again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was narrowed. They dilated it to 4mm. No complications during the procedure. Your oxygen levels stayed stable, and your chest X-ray afterward was clear — no pneumothorax or fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. The pain is manageable, but oxycodone usually works better than Tylenol for me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. We’ll keep you on oxycodone 5mg every six hours as needed. You’re on 40% trach mask now, and your saturations are 98%, which is excellent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I took all my morning meds today — prednisone, losartan, the Esbriet, and the inhaled tobramycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll continue all your home medications. The Esbriet dose is being gradually increased, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m on the third step — three capsules three times a day now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. That’s for the lung fibrosis related to your ___ syndrome. We’re also continuing your prednisone for the relapsing polychondritis. You’re on 7.5mg daily, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I know I’ve been on it a long time. I’m careful about not missing doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. Because you’re on chronic steroids, your body may not respond well during an illness. If you get sick — fever, nausea, vomiting — you’ll need to triple your dose for three days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from last time. What if I can’t take the pill?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re sending you home with a Solu-Cortef injection — 100mg. If you’re unconscious, severely ill, or can’t swallow, someone can give you that shot and you must go to the ER immediately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s reassuring. Should I get a MedicAlert bracelet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we strongly recommend it. It could save your life in an emergency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m back to check on your pain. How’s it been since your last dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. The oxycodone helped. Still a dull ache, but no sharp pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep monitoring. Your labs came back — white count is a bit high at 18.6, but that’s likely from inflammation or your chronic condition, not infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the polychondritis or the pseudomonas?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely the inflammation. You’re colonized with pseudomonas, so we’re continuing inhaled tobramycin, but there’s no sign of active infection this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my GERD? I’ve been using famotidine daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re keeping you on famotidine. Controlling acid reflux helps protect your airway, especially with your trach and history of narrowing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just reviewing your chest X-ray from this morning — it shows some bibasilar atelectasis, meaning the lower parts of your lungs are a bit collapsed. But no pneumonia or pneumothorax.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be doing more with the incentive spirometer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Keep using it every hour while awake. Deep breaths help re-expand those areas. The physical therapist will stop by later to assist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s your voice? I notice you’re whispering.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still hoarse. I haven’t had a real voice since the trach. But I can communicate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understandable. The procedure focused on the lower airways, so your voice may not change much. But we’ll monitor for any swelling or irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’ve made it through the night well. Vital signs are stable — pulse 84, BP 132/73, oxygen 100% on trach mask.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Morning. I feel ready to go home. Pain is minimal now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you today. You’ll go home with six oxycodone tablets for breakthrough pain — take one every six hours as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Only six? What if the pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pain should improve over the next few days. If it doesn’t, or if you need more meds, call your pulmonologist. This is just a short course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have an appointment with interventional pulmonology in four weeks. Your rheumatology follow-up was rescheduled for next week — they’ll manage your polychondritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ll make sure to keep both.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your regular meds: prednisone, losartan, Esbriet, tobramycin, and famotidine. And remember — triple your steroid dose if you get sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And use the injection if I can’t take the pill. I’ll get the MedicAlert bracelet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Call your pulmonologist immediately if you develop shortness of breath, wheezing, or trouble with your trach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for all the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You did well. We’ll have the discharge papers ready soon, and you should be home within a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before discharge. You’re alert, breathing comfortably, and your exam is stable. We’re clearing you to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Here’s your discharge summary. It explains why you were here, what was done, and what to do next.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ll read it carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing — stay hydrated, rest, and don’t push yourself. Healing takes time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll take it easy. Appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___. We’re here if you need us.
